proposals.relationship: De Vries credits Brewer’s material culture and consumption seminar invitation with reactivating his household research and leading to his first Western industrious revolution articles.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008 preface xi recounts returning to a research interest first developed during his dissertation after Brewer’s 1990 invitation. It also credits the distinct 1986 conversation with Akira Hayami that made him receptive to the invitation. The claim is a concrete scholarly stimulus, beyond mere attendance, not sole origin, coauthorship of all subsequent work or adoption of every cultural history position. Hayami’s stronger conceptual contribution is held for a missing endpoint; original seminar exchanges remain unread.
primary_locators: 2008 preface and acknowledgments xi, paragraph beginning I have been thinking; actual frontmatter PDF leaf10 visually collated

proposals.relationship: De Vries explicitly describes Wrigley’s work as a scholarly standard he has striven to attain throughout his career.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008 preface xi ties Wrigley’s 2000 McArthur lecture invitation to this explicit acknowledgment, then credits the wider learned and critical Cambridge audience for clarifying how to turn the lectures into the book. This supports an acknowledged intellectual model, not formal supervision or attribution of the entire household theory to Wrigley. Own 1994 page252 jointly credits demographic resources including Wrigley and Schofield; that co-credit and the existing broad demography routes remain. The reverse Wrigley use of de Vries and van der Woude, edge2623, is a separate empirical appropriation.
primary_locators: 2008 preface xi, final paragraph; following xii audience credits

proposals.relationship: De Vries challenges the sufficiency of an imposed work discipline account associated with Thompson when explaining increased early modern labor, stressing household consumption incentives while retaining exploitation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1994 page258 places Thompson’s specific work discipline quotation within a criticism of portraying workers as initially nonacquisitive and in need of training as both workers and consumers. Note26 cites Time, Work, Discipline,90, visually checked in the actual article. The adjacent Pollard quotation is a separate co-target. De Vries then contrasts literary and historical evidence of material aspirations, but page260 explicitly recognizes self-exploitation of wives and children, lost leisure and other social harms. This records his bounded disagreement, not proof that Thompson denied every consumer motive or that increased labor was universally free or beneficial. Original Thompson essay and historical witnesses remain unread.

proposals.relationship: De Vries criticizes Stearns’s definition of consumerism for its conceptual shortcomings while also directing readers to Stearns’s historiographical overview.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008 page5 note13 calls Stearns’s Consumerism in World History definition remarkable chiefly for its shortcomings. He separately criticizes Steven Miles’s distinction between consumption and consumerism and insists on distinguishing acquisition from final consumption and allowing multiple dimensions of utility. The note ends with Stearns’s 1997 periodization overview as a reading reference. This is a particular definitional criticism, not rejection of all Stearns scholarship; Miles’s argument and the broader critique are not silently assigned solely to Stearns. Neither original Stearns nor Miles text newly read.
